sections.title: DRY: Single Source of Truth for Knowledge
sections.content: **DRY** (Don't Repeat Yourself) is a design principle that says every piece of **business logic, validation rule, or knowledge** should exist in exactly one place in your codebase. When you violate DRY, you create multiple sources of truth. If a requirement changes, you must hunt down all duplicates and update them — and you will inevitably miss one, leading to inconsistent behavior and bugs. Think of it like keeping your phone number in one contact list versus writing it on five sticky notes. If your number changes, updating one list is easy; finding all five sticky notes is error-prone. DRY is not about avoiding all repetition — it is about avoiding **knowledge duplication**. The same SQL query string repeated in three methods is a DRY violation. Two methods that happen to have similar-looking loops but serve entirely different purposes is not a violation. The goal is **maintainability**: change a rule once, and the change propagates automatically because there is only one place where that rule lives.

sections.title: DRY Violation and Fix in Order Validation
Key Points
content: **Knowledge duplication**: DRY is about duplicating business rules or logic, not just code text that happens to look similar
**Single source of truth**: each piece of knowledge should have exactly one authoritative representation in the system
**Maintenance cost**: duplicated logic requires multiple updates when requirements change, increasing bug risk
**WET antipattern**: Write Everything Twice or We Enjoy Typing is the opposite of DRY and leads to inconsistent behavior
**Accidental duplication**: code that looks similar but serves different purposes should not be forced into shared abstractions
**Configuration and constants**: magic numbers, connection strings, and validation rules are common DRY violations
**Database schema**: column names, table structures, and constraints should not be duplicated across queries and code

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. It means every piece of business logic or knowledge should live in exactly one place in your code. If you duplicate logic, changing that logic later requires updating multiple places, and you'll almost certainly miss one. That creates bugs. For example, imagine you're validating order totals in a Spring Boot app. If you copy-paste the same validation check into createOrder, updateOrder, and processRefund methods, that's a DRY violation. When the business changes the rule from total must be positive to total must be at least ten dollars, you have to find and update three places. Miss one and you've got inconsistent behavior. The fix is simple: extract the validation into a single validateOrderTotal method and call it from all three places. Now the rule lives in one spot. Change it once and it's fixed everywhere. One thing to watch out for: DRY is about knowledge duplication, not text duplication. If two pieces of code happen to look similar but represent different business concepts, don't force them together. That's over-applying DRY and it creates bad abstractions. We sometimes call the opposite of DRY the WET antipattern: Write Everything Twice or We Enjoy Typing. You don't want that.

sections.title: KISS: Simplicity as a Design Goal
sections.content: **KISS** (Keep It Simple, Stupid) is a principle that says **the simplest solution that solves the problem is usually the best solution**. Developers, especially early in their careers, often fall into the trap of over-engineering: adding layers of abstraction, using complex design patterns, or building elaborate frameworks when a straightforward approach would work perfectly. This happens because complexity feels impressive and simple code feels too easy. But complexity has a cost: it makes code harder to understand, harder to debug, harder to test, and harder to change. A junior developer can understand simple code. Only the original author can understand over-engineered code, and often not even them after six months. Think of KISS as **maximizing readability and minimizing cognitive load**. If you can solve a problem with a 10-line method instead of a 5-class hierarchy, choose the 10-line method. You are not being lazy — you are being disciplined. Antoine de Saint-Exupéry said perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away. That is KISS in one sentence.

sections.title: KISS Violation and Simplification in User Lookup
Key Points
content: **Simplest solution wins**: if two solutions both work, choose the one that is easier to understand and maintain
**Cognitive load**: complex code requires more mental effort to read, debug, and change, slowing down the entire team
**Premature abstraction**: adding design patterns or layers before you need them is over-engineering and violates KISS
**Readability first**: code is read 10 times more often than it is written, optimize for the reader not the writer
**Not laziness**: choosing simplicity requires discipline and restraint, it is harder than adding complexity
**Less code, fewer bugs**: the best code is no code, every line is a liability that can contain a bug
**Refactor toward simplicity**: if you cannot explain your solution in two sentences, it is probably too complex

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: KISS stands for Keep It Simple, Stupid, though some people say Keep It Short and Simple. The idea is that the simplest solution that works is usually the best one. When you're writing code, it's really tempting to add layers of abstraction, use fancy design patterns, or build elaborate frameworks. That feels smart. But complexity has a real cost. It makes your code harder to read, harder to debug, and harder to change. Let's say you need to look up a user by email in a Spring Boot app. You could create a UserLookupStrategy interface, build EmailLookupStrategy and UsernameLookupStrategy implementations, wire them up with dependency injection, and feel very clever. Or you could just call userRepository.findByEmail directly in your service. That's KISS. The second version does exactly the same thing but it's ten times easier to understand. A junior dev joining your team can read it immediately. The over-engineered version requires them to trace through three files just to figure out what's happening. One thing to remember: KISS is not about being lazy. Choosing simplicity actually requires discipline. It's easy to add complexity. It's hard to keep things simple. There's a famous quote: perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away. That's KISS in one sentence.

beats.content: YAGNI stands for You Aren't Gonna Need It. The principle says: don't implement a feature until you actually have a requirement for it. Every line of code you add must be maintained, tested, and understood by everyone who works on the codebase.

A classic YAGNI violation is building a plugin architecture for a payment system when there's only one payment provider and no plans for more. You spent two weeks building something nobody asked for, it adds complexity, and requirements change anyway so it may never be used.

sharp edge: YAGNI isn't about not thinking ahead. You still design your code to be extensible. But extensible design doesn't mean implementing all possible extensions now. It means writing code that's easy to extend later, when the requirement is actually real.

sections.title: YAGNI: Build Only What You Need Today
sections.content: **YAGNI** (You Aren't Gonna Need It) is a principle from **Extreme Programming** that says: do not implement functionality until it is actually required. Developers often try to anticipate future needs and build features in advance. This seems smart, but it usually backfires. Most of the time, those hypothetical future requirements never materialize, or they materialize in a completely different form than you predicted. Now you have dead code sitting in your codebase — code that adds complexity, increases surface area for bugs, and makes the system harder to understand. Even worse, that code is untested in production because nobody is using it yet. Think of YAGNI as **deferring decisions until you have real information**. Instead of building a flexible notification system that supports email, SMS, push notifications, and carrier pigeons, build email support when you need email. Add SMS when you actually need SMS. Each feature should be driven by a real, current requirement. This is the heart of **agile and iterative development**: build, ship, learn, then build the next thing. YAGNI keeps your codebase lean and forces you to solve real problems instead of imaginary ones.

sections.title: YAGNI Violation and Fix in Notification System
Key Points
content: **No speculative features**: do not build functionality for hypothetical future requirements that may never come
**Dead code cost**: unneeded features add complexity, increase bug surface area, and make the codebase harder to navigate
**Prediction failure**: most future requirements you anticipate never materialize, or arrive in a different form than expected
**Untested code**: features built before they are needed are not tested in production and often do not work when finally used
**Agile alignment**: YAGNI is core to iterative development — build, ship, learn, then add the next feature based on real feedback
**Defer decisions**: make architectural decisions as late as possible when you have the most information
**Not about planning**: YAGNI means do not implement speculative features, not do not think about the future or design for change

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: YAGNI stands for You Aren't Gonna Need It. The principle is simple: don't add functionality until you actually need it. It's really tempting to anticipate future requirements and build features in advance. You think you're being smart and forward-thinking. But most of the time, those future requirements never actually happen. Or they happen in a completely different way than you predicted. Now you've got dead code sitting in your system. That code adds complexity, creates more surface area for bugs, and makes the codebase harder to understand. Even worse, it's not tested in production because nobody is using it yet. Let me give you an example. Say you're building a notification system for a Spring Boot app. Today you only need email notifications. But you think in the future we might need SMS, push notifications, maybe webhooks. So you build a big flexible NotificationService with a Channel enum and a switch statement handling all four types. That's a YAGNI violation. Three of those four channels are hypothetical. Instead, just build sendEmail today. When you actually get a requirement for SMS, add sendSMS then. That's YAGNI. It's core to agile development: build, ship, learn, then add the next thing. One important clarification: YAGNI is not about not planning ahead. You should absolutely think about the future and design for change. YAGNI just means don't implement features until you need them.

sections.title: How DRY, KISS, and YAGNI Form a Unified Philosophy
sections.content: **DRY**, **KISS**, and **YAGNI** are not three random unrelated rules — they form a **unified philosophy of code quality**. Each addresses a different dimension of the same underlying goal: keeping your codebase lean, understandable, and maintainable. **DRY** (Don't Repeat Yourself) tackles **maintainability** by eliminating knowledge duplication. **KISS** (Keep It Simple, Stupid) tackles **readability** by eliminating unnecessary complexity. **YAGNI** (You Aren't Gonna Need It) tackles **simplicity over time** by eliminating premature features. Together, they push you toward the same destination: **minimal, clear, single-purpose code**. When you follow all three, you end up with a codebase where every line has a reason to exist, every piece of logic lives in one place, and every solution is as simple as it can be. They also reinforce each other. YAGNI prevents you from building complex abstractions you don't need, which helps you follow KISS. KISS keeps your code simple, which makes it easier to spot DRY violations. DRY reduces duplication, which keeps the codebase small and helps you follow YAGNI.

sections.title: When to Apply Each Principle
sections.content: Apply **DRY** when you notice the same business logic, validation rule, or calculation appearing in multiple places. Extract it into a single function or configuration. Apply **KISS** when you are about to add a design pattern, abstraction layer, or framework because it feels clever. Ask yourself: is this complexity necessary to solve the current problem? If not, choose the simpler solution. Apply **YAGNI** when you are tempted to build functionality for a hypothetical future requirement. Ask yourself: do I have a concrete, current need for this feature right now? If not, defer it until you do. Use them together as a **decision filter**: before adding any code, ask (1) does this duplicate existing knowledge (DRY), (2) is this more complex than necessary (KISS), and (3) is this solving a real problem today (YAGNI). If you answer yes to any of those questions, stop and rethink your approach.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Unified goal**: all three principles push toward lean, maintainable, readable code that solves real problems
**Different dimensions**: DRY is about duplication, KISS is about complexity, YAGNI is about premature features
**Reinforce each other**: following one principle often makes it easier to follow the others
**Decision filter**: use all three as a checklist before adding any code to the system
**Not rigid rules**: they are guidelines that require judgment and context, not absolute laws
**Team alignment**: all three principles are easier to follow when the whole team values simplicity and maintainability
**Agile philosophy**: together they embody the agile mindset of building iteratively based on real feedback

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: DRY, KISS, and YAGNI aren't three separate unrelated rules. They're actually three parts of the same philosophy. They each address a different dimension of code quality, but they're all pushing you toward the same goal: lean, maintainable code. DRY is about maintainability. It says don't duplicate knowledge because duplication creates inconsistency and makes changes harder. KISS is about readability. It says keep your solutions simple because complexity makes code hard to understand and debug. YAGNI is about simplicity over time. It says don't build features until you need them because speculative code is dead weight. Here's how they work together. Imagine you're building a payment system and you think you might need to support credit cards, PayPal, and cryptocurrency in the future. So you build an elaborate PaymentStrategy interface with three implementations, even though today you only process credit cards. That violates YAGNI. You also add complex validation logic for crypto wallets that's duplicated across two classes. That violates DRY. And the whole thing is way more complex than it needs to be for just credit cards. That violates KISS. The fix is to follow all three. Build only credit card processing today because that's what you need right now. That's YAGNI. Keep it simple with a single validateCreditCard method. That's KISS. Put that validation in one place. That's DRY. Now you've got minimal, clear code that does exactly what's needed and nothing more.

beats.content: DRY can be over-applied when you confuse accidental similarity with real duplication. Two methods that happen to look alike right now aren't necessarily representing the same knowledge. They might evolve in completely different directions.

If you extract them into a shared utility prematurely, you've coupled two unrelated concerns. When one needs to change, you're forced to also affect the other, or you add awkward flags to distinguish the cases. The coupling is worse than the original duplication.

question: Can DRY be over-applied? When does abstraction hurt?
title: When DRY goes too far — premature abstraction
direct_answer: Yes. Over-applying DRY leads to premature abstraction — creating shared utilities for code that happens to look similar but serves different purposes. If two pieces of code are accidentally similar today but will evolve differently, forcing them into a shared abstraction creates coupling that hurts later. The Rule of Three is a practical guide: duplicate once, abstract on the third occurrence.

sections.title: When DRY Becomes a Problem
sections.content: **DRY is a guideline, not an absolute law**. Over-applying it is one of the most common mistakes developers make, especially when they first learn the principle. The problem happens when you see two pieces of code that look similar and immediately extract them into a shared abstraction — but those two pieces of code are only **accidentally similar**. They happen to have the same structure today, but they represent different business concepts and will evolve in different directions. By forcing them into a shared abstraction, you create **coupling**: now changes to one concept require touching shared code that affects the other concept. This is worse than duplication. Think of it like this: duplication is a maintenance problem (you have to change code in two places), but premature abstraction is an **architectural problem** (you cannot change one thing without risking breaking another). The **Rule of Three** is a pragmatic heuristic: the first time you write code, just write it. The second time you write similar code, you're allowed to duplicate it. The third time, stop and consider whether this is real duplication or accidental similarity. If it's real, abstract. If not, leave it duplicated. Some teams even follow **WET** (Write Everything Twice) intentionally: allow duplication up to two occurrences before abstracting.

sections.title: Premature Abstraction Hurting Flexibility
Key Points
content: **Accidental similarity**: code that looks the same but serves different purposes should not be forced into shared abstractions
**Coupling cost**: premature abstraction creates dependencies between unrelated concepts that will diverge over time
**Rule of Three**: duplicate once, duplicate twice, abstract on the third occurrence when you're sure it's real duplication
**WET principle**: Write Everything Twice is a pragmatic approach that allows duplication until you're certain abstraction is correct
**Evolution divergence**: if two pieces of code will change for different reasons, keep them separate even if they look similar
**Knowledge vs structure**: DRY is about duplicating business knowledge, not about duplicating code structure or syntax patterns
**Refactor later**: it's easier to extract an abstraction from duplicated code later than to split a bad abstraction apart

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Yes, DRY can definitely be over-applied. The problem happens when you treat it as an absolute law instead of a guideline. You see two pieces of code that look similar and you immediately think I have to extract this into a shared method. But sometimes that similarity is accidental. The two pieces of code happen to have the same structure today, but they represent different business concepts and they're going to evolve in different directions. Let me give you an example. Say you're formatting customer names in a report and you're also formatting user names in emails. Both are concatenating first name and last name with a space. They look identical. If you extract that into a shared formatName utility, you've created coupling. Later the business says reports need to show names as last-name-comma-first-name. Now you're stuck. You can't change the shared utility without breaking emails. You've made it harder to change either piece of code independently. That's worse than duplication. There's a pragmatic heuristic called the Rule of Three. The first time you write some code, just write it. The second time you write similar code, you're allowed to duplicate it. The third time, stop and ask yourself: is this real knowledge duplication or accidental similarity? If it's real, abstract it. If not, leave it separate. Some teams even follow WET, which stands for Write Everything Twice. Allow duplication up to two occurrences before you abstract. The key insight is that it's easier to extract an abstraction from duplicated code later than it is to split apart a bad abstraction. Duplication is a maintenance problem. Premature abstraction is an architectural problem.
